method: S1, S2 and S3 are OPEN articles, fetched and checked verbatim. S1 is Australian Prescriber 2005, S2 Australian Prescriber 2021, S3 RACGP Australian Family Physician 2016. A1 is AMH, read under subscription and PARAPHRASED: no passage reproduced, no source_text stored, locator plus verdict licensed_source_not_quoted; doses flagged dose:true. Edition 1.1 added S3, which FILLED a hole 1.0 recorded (no description of the Epley manoeuvre) and SURFACED four disagreements between sources. Where sources disagree the guideline attributes each statement to the source that makes it and does NOT resolve the disagreement; claims that exist only to record what one source says are worded 'S3 states that ...' so the claim is true even where the underlying assertion is contested. S3 also contradicts ITSELF on Dix-Hallpike nystagmus (horizontal in its table, rotational in its BPPV text) and both statements are quoted separately.

claims.claim: Dizziness covers a range of symptoms and is rarely a sign of a serious disorder
claims.source_text: Dizziness is a term used to describe a range of symptoms, but is rarely a sign of a serious disorder.

claims.claim: The common causes of vertigo are benign positional vertigo, Meniere's syndrome, vestibular neuritis and migraine
claims.source_text: The common causes of vertigo are benign positional vertigo, Meniere's syndrome, vestibular neuritis and migraine.

claims.claim: Vertigo is usually provoked or aggravated by movement and relieved by rest, whereas dizziness unaltered by resting or moving is usually non-vestibular
claims.source_text: Dizziness of vestibular origin (vertigo) is usually provoked or aggravated by movement and improved or relieved by rest (sitting or lying down). … dizziness which is unaltered between resting and moving about is usually non-vestibular in origin

claims.claim: Dizziness which precedes a blackout or near blackout usually indicates a syncopal or presyncopal disorder requiring a different approach
claims.source_text: Dizziness which precedes a blackout or near blackout will usually indicate a syncopal/presyncopal disorder which requires a different approach.

claims.claim: Drugs that can cause dizziness include antihypertensives, anticonvulsants, antidepressants and sedatives, acting through postural hypotension or direct vestibular effects
claims.source_text: Drugs which can cause dizziness include antihypertensives, anticonvulsants, antidepressants and sedatives. The dizziness occurs either through postural hypotension or direct effects on the central or peripheral vestibular system.

claims.claim: Deafness, tinnitus and aural fullness suggest a labyrinthine cause; headache, diplopia, paraesthesiae, weakness, dysarthria or dysphagia suggest a neurological cause
claims.source_text: symptoms such as deafness, tinnitus and aural fullness or pressure might suggest a labyrinthine cause, whereas symptoms such as headache, diplopia, facial/limb paraesthesiae, weakness or clumsiness, dysarthria or dysphagia might suggest a neurological cause

claims.claim: Duration separates the causes: under a minute in benign positional vertigo, minutes in TIA, minutes to hours in migraine and Meniere's, more than 24 hours in vestibular neuronitis or posterior circulation stroke
claims.source_text: Vertigo lasts less than one minute in benign positional vertigo, minutes in transient ischaemic attacks, minutes to hours in migraine and Ménière's syndrome and for more than 24 hours in vestibular neuronitis or posterior circulation stroke.

claims.claim: Recurrent isolated vertigo is usually peripheral and benign but not always; central vestibular disorders include brainstem lesions and multiple sclerosis
claims.source_text: Although recurrent isolated vertigo is usually peripheral and benign, this is not always the case. Central vestibular disorders include brainstem lesions and multiple sclerosis.

claims.claim: A patient with dizziness requires thorough neurological, otological and cardiovascular examination including supine and upright blood pressure
claims.source_text: A patient with dizziness requires a thorough neurological, otological and cardiovascular examination, including supine and upright blood pressure measurements, particularly if the cause of the dizziness is not apparent from the history.

claims.claim: Purely vertical or torsional nystagmus suggests a central lesion; mixed horizontal/torsional nystagmus suggests a peripheral vestibular cause
claims.source_text: Purely vertical or torsional nystagmus suggests a central lesion, whereas a mixed horizontal/torsional nystagmus suggests peripheral vestibular nystagmus.

claims.claim: Peripheral vestibular nystagmus beats in the same direction regardless of eye position; nystagmus that changes direction with gaze may indicate a central neurological lesion
claims.source_text: Peripheral vestibular nystagmus produces a nystagmus which beats in the same direction regardless of the eye position. Nystagmus which changes direction with different eye positions (for example, beating to the right on right gaze and then beating to the left on left gaze) may indicate a central neurological lesion.

claims.claim: Peripheral vestibular nystagmus is attenuated by visual fixation, so it may not be detected by conventional examination
claims.source_text: The nystagmus of peripheral vestibular disorders tends to be attenuated by visual fixation and so nystagmus may not be detected in the conventional manner in these patients.

claims.claim: Nystagmus from vestibular neuritis is obvious acutely but in many cases rapidly attenuates over 24-48 hours
claims.source_text: Acute severe vestibular insults such as vestibular neuritis may produce nystagmus, which is obvious in the acute phase, but in many cases this rapidly attenuates over 24-48 hours.

claims.claim: The head-impulse test asks the patient to fixate on the examiner's nose while the head is rapidly rotated to either side, after excluding significant neck problems; in healthy people the eyes stay fixed
claims.source_text: This test involves asking the patient to fixate on the examiner's nose. The examiner then rapidly rotates the patient's head to either side (after excluding any significant neck problem). … In healthy people the eyes remain fixed on the examiner's nose regardless of the head position.

claims.claim: In a labyrinthine lesion the eyes move with the head towards the side of the lesion and a quick corrective eye movement follows; that corrective movement is the abnormality sought
claims.source_text: In a patient with a labyrinthine lesion, the eyes will move with the head when turned to the side of the lesion and then after a short delay the visual system will trigger a quick corrective eye movement back to the examiner's nose. This quick corrective eye movement is the abnormality sought when undertaking the test.

claims.claim: The head-impulse test is positive in vestibular neuritis but negative with a cerebellar infarct
claims.source_text: The head-impulse test is also useful in the differential diagnosis of cerebellar infarcts and vestibular neuritis. The test is positive in vestibular neuritis, but negative with a cerebellar infarct.

claims.claim: In bilateral peripheral vestibular impairment dynamic visual acuity often drops several lines from static, for example 6/6 to 6/36 or 6/60; normal dynamic acuity does not rule out a unilateral lesion
claims.source_text: In patients with bilateral peripheral vestibular impairment the visual acuity often drops several lines from the static to dynamic condition, for example from 6/6 to 6/36 or 6/60. … Normal dynamic visual acuity does not rule out a unilateral vestibular lesion.

claims.claim: The Hallpike manoeuvre should be performed if there is any hint of positional vertigo and in all patients with no obvious cause for their symptoms
claims.source_text: The manoeuvre should therefore be performed if there is any hint of positional vertigo and in all patients where there is no obvious cause for their symptoms.

claims.claim: In the Hallpike manoeuvre the patient is rapidly moved from sitting to supine with the head hanging over the end of the couch or a pillow behind the shoulders, then the test is repeated with the head turned the other way
claims.source_text: The patient is then rapidly moved into a supine position on the examination couch with the head hanging over the end of the couch or a pillow placed behind the shoulders. … Then the test is repeated with the patient's head turned to the opposite side.

claims.claim: A positive Hallpike shows, after a latency of up to several seconds, torsional/vertical nystagmus beating towards the lower ear with vertigo, locating the lesion to the lower ear
claims.source_text: Typically a patient with benign positional vertigo will develop, after a short latency of up to several seconds, a torsional/vertical nystagmus with fast phases directed towards the lower ear accompanied by vertigo. This means the lesion is on the side of the lower ear.

claims.claim: In patients with recurrent isolated vertigo and normal hearing there is a low yield from imaging, particularly for cerebellopontine angle tumours
claims.source_text: in patients with recurrent isolated vertigo and normal hearing, there is a low yield from imaging studies particularly in regard to cerebellopontine angle tumours or masses

claims.claim: There is no singularly effective pharmacological treatment to abolish vertigo
claims.source_text: There is no singularly effective pharmacological treatment to abolish vertigo

claims.claim: A patient can be supported through an acute episode with short-term vestibular sedatives such as benzodiazepines, antihistamines or prochlorperazine, plus antiemetics and bed rest
claims.source_text: a patient can be supported through an acute episode of vertigo with short-term use of vestibular sedatives such as benzodiazepines, antihistamines or prochlorperazine. Antiemetics and bed rest are also useful.

claims.claim: The efficacy evidence for vestibular sedatives comes from laboratory animal research; clinical observation of efficacy is anecdotal and there are no controlled trials
claims.source_text: The evidence of efficacy of the vestibular sedatives is based on experimental laboratory animal research which shows reduced vestibular neural activity in response to these drugs. Clinical observation of this efficacy is anecdotal and there are no controlled trials.

claims.claim: Patients with chronic or recurring vertigo are commonly treated with betahistine and/or prochlorperazine although there is no evidence of the drugs' long-term efficacy
claims.source_text: Patients with chronic or recurring vertigo are commonly treated with betahistine and/or prochlorperazine although there is no evidence of the drugs' long-term efficacy.

claims.claim: Patients with chronic or recurring vertigo often do well with vestibular adaptation exercises or a formal vestibular rehabilitation program
claims.source_text: These patients will often do well with vestibular adaptation exercises or a formal vestibular rehabilitation program to help manage their symptoms.

claims.claim: Drugs prescribed for acute vertigo should be used sparingly as they may impair the vestibular adaptation process
claims.source_text: The drugs prescribed for acute vertigo should be used sparingly as they may impair the vestibular adaptation process.

claims.claim: SSRIs such as sertraline may have a role in the management of vertigo but have not been extensively studied
claims.source_text: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors such as sertraline may have a role in the management of vertigo, however, they have not been extensively studied.

claims.claim: The most effective treatment of vertigo is treatment of the specific cause if it can be identified
claims.source_text: The most effective treatment of vertigo is treatment of the specific cause if it can be identified

claims.claim: Particle repositioning manoeuvres for benign positional vertigo are 80-90% effective after a single manoeuvre against a spontaneous recovery rate of about 50% over six weeks
claims.source_text: The particle repositioning manoeuvres for benign positional vertigo are 80-90% effective following a single manoeuvre compared to a spontaneous recovery rate of approximately 50% over six weeks.

claims.claim: Benign positional vertigo can be treated with simple physical manoeuvres although recurrences are frequent; Brandt-Daroff positional exercises are a possible alternative
claims.source_text: Benign positional vertigo can be treated with simple physical manoeuvres, although recurrences are frequent. … The Brandt-Daroff positional exercises are a possible alternative treatment.

claims.claim: Migraine is an important diagnostic consideration in dizziness whether or not there is an accompanying headache
claims.source_text: Migraine is an important diagnostic consideration in patients presenting with dizziness, whether they have an accompanying headache or not.

claims.claim: In Meniere's syndrome the majority of patients respond to conservative management including a low salt diet and possibly diuretics
claims.source_text: the majority of patients will respond to conservative medical management including a low salt diet and possibly diuretics

claims.claim: Short-term corticosteroids may be useful in refractory Meniere's syndrome with relatively preserved hearing
claims.source_text: Short-term corticosteroids may be useful in refractory cases with relatively preserved hearing.

claims.claim: Intra-tympanic gentamicin and surgery are reserved for refractory Meniere's cases unresponsive to other measures with significant hearing loss
claims.source_text: More aggressive therapies such as intra-tympanic gentamicin and/or surgery are reserved for refractory cases unresponsive to other measures and where there is significant hearing loss.

claims.claim: An acute vestibular syndrome resembling vestibular neuritis may be a manifestation of cerebrovascular disease, and increased diagnostic suspicion is required in older patients with vascular risk factors
claims.source_text: An acute vestibular syndrome resembling vestibular neuritis and recurrent brief isolated vertigo may occur as manifestations of cerebrovascular disease. Increased diagnostic suspicion is required in older patients with associated vascular risk factors.

claims.claim: Vertigo has peripheral causes such as labyrinthitis and central causes such as cerebellar ischaemia, or a mixture; treatment should be aimed at the cause
claims.source_text: Vertigo has a variety of causes. These may be peripheral, such as labyrinthitis, or central, such as cerebellar ischaemia, or a mixture of the two. The treatment of vertigo should be aimed at the cause, but a variety of drugs has been used to relieve the symptom.

claims.claim: Cinnarizine inhibits H1, H4 and dopamine D2 receptors and can block calcium channels; dimenhydrinate releases diphenhydramine, inhibits H1 and muscarinic receptors and enters the brain, so the combination has peripheral and central effects
claims.source_text: Cinnarizine inhibits histamine H 1 and H 4 receptors and dopamine D 2 receptors. It can also block calcium channels. Dimenhydrinate is a salt of diphenhydramine and chlorotheophylline. It inhibits histamine H 1 receptors and muscarinic acetylcholine receptors and can enter the brain. The combination of cinnarizine and dimenhydrinate will therefore have peripheral and central effects.

claims.claim: Both drugs are metabolised mainly by CYP2D6, with potential to interact with other CYP2D6 substrates such as antidepressants and beta blockers
claims.source_text: They are metabolised mainly by cytochrome P450 (CYP) 2D6 in the liver. There may be a potential to interact with other drugs metabolised by CYP2D6, such as antidepressants and beta blockers.

claims.claim: The combination is contraindicated in severe hepatic or renal impairment
claims.source_text: The combination is therefore contraindicated in patients with severe hepatic or renal impairment.

claims.claim: An analysis of five double-blind randomised trials involved 635 patients of average age 53 years, most with vertigo for more than one year, taking the drugs three times a day for four weeks
claims.source_text: An analysis of five of the double-blind, randomised trials involved 635 patients with an average age of 53 years. Most of them had experienced vertigo for more than one year. … The drugs were taken three times a day for four weeks.

claims.claim: More than 68% taking the combination felt much or very much improved, against 33% of the betahistine group and 35% of the placebo group
claims.source_text: More than 68% of the patients felt much improved or very much improved after taking the combination compared with 33% of the betahistine group and 35% of the placebo group.

claims.claim: In the pooled five-trial table betahistine 12 mg reduced the vertigo score by 5.7 in 40 patients while placebo reduced it by 6.4 in 51 patients
claims.source_text: Betahistine 12 mg 40 5.7 … Placebo 51 6.4

claims.claim: In the same table the combination reduced the score by 13.6, cinnarizine 20 mg by 11.5 and dimenhydrinate 40 mg by 11.4
claims.source_text: Cinnarizine 20 mg/dimenhydrinate 40 mg 196 13.6 … Cinnarizine 20 mg 60 11.5 … Dimenhydrinate 40 mg 59 11.4

claims.claim: In the same table the higher single-agent doses performed worse than the lower ones: cinnarizine 50 mg reduced the score by 7.8 and dimenhydrinate 100 mg by 7.3
claims.source_text: Cinnarizine 50 mg 98 7.8 … Dimenhydrinate 100 mg 97 7.3

claims.claim: A later double-blind trial in 306 patients with peripheral vestibular vertigo excluded confirmed Meniere's disease although about 55% had a Meniere-like symptom complex
claims.source_text: A more recent double-blind trial compared the combination to betahistine in 306 patients with peripheral vestibular vertigo. Approximately 55% of the patients had a Ménière-like symptom complex, but patients with confirmed Ménière's disease were excluded.

claims.claim: In that trial the composite vertigo score declined 67.5% with the combination and 59.5% with betahistine after four weeks, with about 71% versus 63% much or very much improved
claims.source_text: After four weeks this composite score had declined by 67.5% in the patients taking the combination and by 59.5% in those taking betahistine. Approximately 71% of the 152 patients randomised to the combination felt much improved or very much improved compared with 63% of the betahistine group.

claims.claim: The most frequent adverse effects were fatigue, somnolence, dry mouth, headache and abdominal pain, and sedation may be increased by alcohol and other CNS depressants
claims.source_text: the most frequent adverse effects seen with the combination of cinnarizine and dimenhydrinate were fatigue, somnolence, dry mouth, headache and abdominal pain. The sedative effects may be increased by other drugs, including alcohol, which depress the central nervous system.

claims.claim: Anticholinergic effects make the combination contraindicated in angle-closure glaucoma and urinary retention, with convulsions, raised intracranial pressure and alcohol abuse also contraindications
claims.source_text: As the combination has some anticholinergic effects, it is contraindicated in patients with angle-closure glaucoma or urinary retention. Convulsions, raised intracranial pressure and alcohol abuse are also contraindications.

claims.claim: Cinnarizine has been associated with extrapyramidal effects including tardive dyskinesia which may be irreversible, so the combination should only be used short term
claims.source_text: Cinnarizine has been associated with extrapyramidal effects including tardive dyskinesia. As these effects may be irreversible, the combination should only be used for short-term management.

claims.claim: The combination has a greater effect than either drug alone but the difference may be small, about two points on the 40-point score against cinnarizine 20 mg, and cinnarizine is not available on its own in Australia
claims.source_text: Combining cinnarizine with dimenhydrinate has a greater effect on vertigo than either drug alone, but the difference may be small. For example, in the five-trial analysis there was a difference of approximately two points between the combination and cinnarizine 20 mg on the 40-point vertigo score … However, cinnarizine is not available on its own in Australia.

claims.claim: In Australia the combination is indicated only for adults who have not responded to other treatments, and given uncertainty about long-term safety treatment should not usually exceed four weeks
claims.source_text: it is only indicated in Australia for adults who have not responded to other treatments. In view of the uncertainty about long-term safety, treatment should not usually exceed four weeks.

claims.claim: Vertigo constitutes approximately 54% of cases of dizziness and classically presents as a sensation of movement of the environment around the patient
claims.source_text: Vertigo is a common, distressing presentation in general practice and constitutes approximately 54% of cases of dizziness. 1 Classically, vertigo presents as a sensation of movement of the environment around the patient.

claims.claim: Dizziness can be classified into four groups: vertigo, disequilibrium, light-headedness and presyncope
claims.source_text: Dizziness can be classified into four groups: - vertigo (spinning sensation) - disequilibrium (feeling of imbalance) - light-headedness (sensation of giddiness) 3 - presyncope (sensation of feeling faint).

claims.claim: Vestibular symptoms originating in the cerebellum or brain stem are central; those arising in the inner ear or vestibular nerve are peripheral
claims.source_text: Vestibular symptoms originating from pathology in the cerebellum or brain stem are classified into the central type. Conversely, symptoms arising in the inner ear or from the vestibular nerve are classified as peripheral.

claims.claim: Central causes are suspected if the patient has associated neurological symptoms such as weakness, dysarthria, sensory changes, ataxia or confusion, and it may be difficult to distinguish central from peripheral when vertigo is the only symptom
claims.source_text: Central causes are suspected if the patient presents with associated neurological symptoms such as weakness, dysarthria, sensory changes, ataxia or confusion. It may be difficult to distinguish between central and peripheral causes in patients who present with vertigo as their only symptom.

claims.claim: Vascular risk factors including smoking, diabetes, obesity, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia need to be assessed to rule out cerebrovascular accident
claims.source_text: Risk factors for vascular disease, including smoking, diabetes, obesity, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia, need to be assessed to rule out CVAs, which can lead to vertigo from ischemia or infarction.

claims.claim: Medications including frusemide, salicylates and antihypertensive agents can affect the vestibular system and cause vertigo, and perilymphatic fistula should be considered after recent head injury
claims.source_text: Medications, including frusemide, salicylates and antihypertensive agents, can affect the vestibular system, which in turn causes vertigo. 10,11 Perilymphatic fistula should be considered if there is a history of recent head injury.

claims.claim: Vertigo with hearing loss is seen in labyrinthitis and Meniere's disease, whereas hearing loss is not seen in benign paroxysmal positional vertigo or vestibular neuronitis
claims.source_text: Vertigo with hearing loss is seen in labyrithitis and Ménière's disease, whereas hearing loss is not seen in benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) and vestibular neuronitis (VN).

claims.claim: Otoscopy should look for vesicles seen in herpes zoster infection or retraction pockets seen in cholesteatoma, and vertigo triggered by pushing on the tragus or by Valsalva suggests a perilymphatic fistula
claims.source_text: an otoscopic examination should be performed to visualise the tympanic membranes for any vesicles that can be seen in a Herpes zoster infection or retraction pockets as seen in cholesteotoma. 2 Vertigo triggered by pushing on the tragus or with the Valsalva manoeuvre is seen in a perilymphatic fistula.

claims.claim: A gait and balance assessment using Romberg's sign and the heel-toe test, with examination for cerebellar signs, can exclude central causes
claims.source_text: A gait and balance assessment (Romberg's sign and the heel-toe test), 12 and examination for cerebellar signs can exclude central causes.

claims.claim: Vertical nystagmus is only seen if the cause is central; central nystagmus may be horizontal, rotational or vertical and does not disappear on fixing the gaze, while peripheral nystagmus disappears with fixation
claims.source_text: Vertical nystagmus is only seen if the cause is central. 7 Nystagmus due to central causes may be horizontal, rotational or vertical, and does not disappear on fixing the gaze. 13 Nystagmus in the peripheral type disappears with fixation of the gaze.

claims.claim: Cardiovascular examination should check pulse, blood pressure, heart rate and rhythm, with carotid examination for bruits
claims.source_text: Cardiovascular examination: pulse, blood pressure, heart rate and rhythm should be checked. 14 Carotid examination to identify bruits (in the case of a CVA) is necessary.

claims.claim: In the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre the head is turned 30 to 45 degrees to the side being tested, the patient keeps their eyes open focused on a stable point, then quickly lies supine and hyperextends the neck, and patients should be warned the test can induce vertigo
claims.source_text: The patient sits at the edge of the bed and the examiner turns the patient's head 30-45 degrees to the side being tested. The patient needs to keep their eyes open and focus on a stable point, and then quickly lie supine and hyperextend the neck. … This test can induce vertigo, so patients should be warned about this before the test is performed.

claims.claim: S3 states that horizontal nystagmus denotes a positive Dix-Hallpike test
claims.source_text: Horizontal nystagmus denotes a positive test.

claims.claim: S3 also states that the nystagmus seen in BPPV has a rotational nature
claims.source_text: Nystagmus seen in BPPV has a rotational nature.

claims.claim: A drop in systolic blood pressure of more than 20 mmHg from lying to standing is significant for a postural drop, seen in dehydration or autonomic dysfunction
claims.source_text: A drop in the systolic blood pressure by more than 20 mm/Hg from a lying down to standing position is significant for a postural drop. This is seen in patients who are dehydrated or who present with autonomic dysfunction.

claims.claim: In S3's description of the head impulse test the examiner quickly turns the head 10 to 20 degrees and the test is abnormal if the eyes move rapidly and repetitively, failing to re-fixate on the examiner's nose, indicating a disrupted vestibulo-ocular reflex
claims.source_text: The patient is asked to look at the examiner's nose and the examiner quickly turns the patient's head 10-20 degrees. It is abnormal if eyes move rapidly and repetitively, failing to re-fixate to the examiner's nose. A positive test indicates disrupted vestibule-ocular reflex.

claims.claim: The most common causes of vertigo in primary care are BPPV, vestibular neuronitis and Meniere's disease
claims.source_text: The most common causes of vertigo seen in primary care are BPPV, VN and Ménière's disease (Table 2).

claims.claim: BPPV is the most common cause of vertigo in clinical practice and is caused by accumulation of calcium crystals in the posterior semicircular canal
claims.source_text: BPPV is the most common cause of vertigo in clinical practice. 15 It is caused by an accumulation of calcium crystals in the posterior semicircular canal.

claims.claim: The Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre is used to diagnose BPPV while the Epley manoeuvre is used to treat it, attempting to dislodge the otoliths from the semicircular canals
claims.source_text: The Dix−Hallpike manoeuvre is used to diagnose BPPV. In contrast, the Epley manoeuvre can be used to treat BPPV (Box 1). 1 This procedure is performed in an attempt to dislodge the otoliths from the semicircular canals.

claims.claim: S3 reports the Epley manoeuvre has a 77% success rate on the initial attempt and 100% on further attempts
claims.source_text: It has a 77% success rate on the initial attempt and 100% on further attempts.

claims.claim: The Epley manoeuvre is performed by sitting the patient on the bed, lying them supine with the neck hyperextended and laterally rotated 45 degrees for one minute, turning the head to the opposite side at 45 degrees for one minute, tilting head chest and pelvis downwards to 135 degrees almost prone for one minute, then quickly sitting the patient upright with the head tilted to the affected side
claims.source_text: - Sit the patient on the bed. - With the neck hyperextended and laterally rotated to 45 degrees, the patient is asked to lie supine. - The patient is required to maintain the supine position for one minute. - The head is turned to the opposite side with lateral rotation of 45 degrees, and remains in this position for one minute. - The head, chest and pelvis are tilted downwards to 135 degrees (almost prone), and this position is maintained for one minute. - Quickly sit the patient upright with their head tilted to the affected side.

claims.claim: The Epley manoeuvre should not be performed in patients with neck injury, carotid stenosis or heart disease
claims.source_text: This manoeuvre should not be performed in patients with neck injury, carotid stenosis and heart disease

claims.claim: Acute labyrinthitis presents with vertigo and hearing loss preceded by a viral infection, lasts days to weeks, and hearing loss is the main distinguishing factor from BPPV
claims.source_text: It presents with vertigo and hearing loss, preceded by a viral infection. 16 Middle ear infections can spread to the inner ear and cause labyrithitis. The duration of symptoms ranges from days to weeks. Hearing loss is the main distinguishing factor between labyrithitis and BPPV.

claims.claim: Typically no treatment is required for labyrinthitis, but if suppurative labyrinthitis is suspected the patient should be referred to the emergency department for drainage of otitis media
claims.source_text: Typically, no treatment is required for labyrithitis. However, if suppurative labyrinthitis is suspected, the patient should be referred to the emergency department for drainage of otitis media.

claims.claim: Meniere's disease classically presents with episodes of vertigo lasting longer than 20 minutes, tinnitus, sensorineural hearing loss and aural fullness, and eventually hearing loss becomes permanent
claims.source_text: Ménière's disease classically presents with episodes of vertigo lasting longer than 20 minutes, tinnitus, sensorineural hearing loss and aural fullness. Eventually, hearing loss becomes permanent. Pure tone audiometry is the most useful test to assess sensorineural hearing loss.

claims.claim: Meniere's disease is commonly seen in women and the incidence increases in men and women after the age of 60 years
claims.source_text: Ménière's disease is commonly seen in women, and the incidence increases in men and women after the age of 60 years.

claims.claim: S3 states there is no known cure for Meniere's disease, treatment is primarily symptomatic, and betahistine is the current mainstay of treatment
claims.source_text: There is no known cure for Ménière's disease and treatment is primarily symptomatic. 19 Betahistine is the current mainstay of treatment.

claims.claim: Vestibular neuronitis follows a viral URTI or herpes zoster infection, presents with acute vertigo without hearing loss or tinnitus, and loss of balance is more prominent than in other causes so patients may present with falls
claims.source_text: The main characteristic of VN is an acute onset of vertigo without hearing loss or tinnitus. … Loss of balance is more prominent in VN, compared with other causes of vertigo, and patients may commonly present with falls.

claims.claim: In vestibular neuronitis the vertigo is initially severe, lasts two to three days and is followed by gradual recovery which may take two to six weeks, with bed rest and antiemetics used in the first 24 to 72 hours
claims.source_text: Initially, the vertigo is severe, lasts for two to three days and is followed by gradual recovery, which may take two to six weeks. 20 Bed rest and antiemetics can be used in the first 24-72 hours.

claims.claim: Blood tests are not routinely ordered for vertigo, but it is recommended that glucose levels of all patients with vertigo should be checked
claims.source_text: Blood tests are not routinely ordered for patients presenting with vertigo. However, it is recommended that glucose levels of all patients with vertigo should be checked.

claims.claim: Imaging with CT, MRI or MRA is indicated if the examination is not consistent with a peripheral lesion, prominent CVA risk factors are present, neurological signs and symptoms are present, or vertigo is accompanied by headache, and referral to a neurologist is recommended in these cases
claims.source_text: Radiological tests including computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) are indicated if: - the examination is not consistent with a peripheral lesion - prominent risk factors for CVA are present - neurological signs and symptoms are present, or - symptoms of vertigo are accompanied by a headache. In these cases, referral to a neurologist is recommended.

claims.claim: S3 describes betahistine as an antiemetic used for symptomatic management of acute vertigo, states these medications should not be used long term, and warns about drowsiness, dry mouth and blurred vision
claims.source_text: Antiemetic medications such as betahistine are used for symptomatic management of acute vertigo. These medications should not be used long term. Patients should be warned about the side effects of drowsiness, dry mouth and blurred vision.

claims.claim: S3 states benzodiazepines are not indicated and should be avoided because of their addictive nature
claims.source_text: Benzodiazepines are not indicated and should be avoided because of their addictive nature.

claims.claim: Lifestyle changes including salt restriction and avoiding alcohol and coffee are recommended, and assessment and management of the patient's risk of falls is important in vertigo
claims.source_text: Lifestyle changes including salt restriction and avoiding alcohol and coffee are recommended. 24 Assessment and management of the patient's risk of falls is important in vertigo.

claims.claim: Referral to an experienced physiotherapist for vestibular rehabilitation can help prevent recurrences, with exercises involving moving the eyes up and down and sideways in a supine or sitting position and balance stabilisation exercises
claims.source_text: Referral to an experienced physiotherapist for vestibular rehabilitation can help prevent recurrences. 16 Exercises prescribed by physiotherapists involve moving the eye balls up and down and sideways in a supine or sitting position. Balance stabilisation exercises help to regain normal activities faster.

claims.claim: Patients should be referred for specialist review if they have continuous vertigo, progressive hearing loss, severe ongoing headache, cerebellar signs or if the diagnosis is not clear
claims.source_text: Patients should be referred for specialist review if they have symptoms of continuous vertigo, progressive hearing loss, severe ongoing headache, cerebellar signs or if the diagnosis is not clear.

claims.claim: Distinguishing peripheral from CNS pathology matters, and hearing loss is usually present in peripheral disease and rare in CNS disease
